In Coding 2 you plotted with base R's `hist()`. Today you will **build figures in layers** with ggplot2.

The first time you click **Run Code**, your browser downloads R once (a few seconds). After that it is quick.

::: {.callout-note}
## The grammar of graphs

Every ggplot2 figure has three essential pieces:

1. **data** — the dataset (for example `penguins`)
2. **aes** — aesthetic mappings: which column goes on which axis, or which color
3. **geom** — the geometric object: points, boxes, bars, histogram bins

You add layers with `+`. We will practice all three today. The two tables below are a reference for this activity and for your assignments.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Common geoms (click to expand)

| Geom | Shows | Needs in `aes()` | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `geom_histogram()` | Distribution of one continuous variable | `x` | `bins = 30` by default; try `binwidth = 100` |
| `geom_density()` | Smoothed outline of a histogram | `x` | |
| `geom_bar()` | Count of rows in each category | `x` (categorical) | Counts for you |
| `geom_col()` | Bars whose heights you already computed | `x`, `y` | |
| `geom_point()` | Scatterplot of two continuous variables | `x`, `y` | |
| `geom_jitter()` | Scatterplot with points nudged apart so they do not overlap | `x`, `y` | `width = 0.2` controls the nudge |
| `geom_boxplot()` | Median, quartiles, and outliers per group | `x` (group), `y` | |
| `geom_violin()` | Full distribution shape per group | `x` (group), `y` | |
| `geom_line()` | Values connected in order along x | `x`, `y` | |
| `geom_smooth()` | A fitted trend line with a confidence band | `x`, `y` | `method = "lm"` for a straight line |
| `geom_errorbar()` | Error bars around a summary | `x`, `ymin`, `ymax` | |

Layers stack with `+` in the order you write them, so `geom_point() + geom_smooth()` draws the line on top of the points.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Aesthetics: what `aes()` can map a column to (click to expand)

| Aesthetic | Controls | Works best with | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x`, `y` | Position on the axes | Any column | `aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)` |
| `color` | Outline or point color | Categories, or a continuous gradient | `aes(color = species)` |
| `fill` | Inside color of bars, boxes, and violins | Categories | `aes(fill = island)` |
| `size` | Point size or line thickness | Continuous | `aes(size = bill_depth_mm)` |
| `shape` | Point shape | Categories (six or fewer) | `aes(shape = sex)` |
| `alpha` | Transparency, 0 to 1 | Continuous, or a fixed value | `geom_point(alpha = 0.5)` |
| `group` | Which rows belong together for lines and boxes | Categories | `aes(group = species)` |

Inside `aes()`, a setting **maps** a column, so each species gets its own color. Outside `aes()`, it **sets** one constant for the whole layer: `geom_point(color = "blue")` makes every point blue.

Helpers you will add to almost every figure: `labs()` for the title and axis labels, `theme_minimal()` for a clean background, and `facet_wrap(~ species)` for one panel per group.

Posit, the company that makes RStudio, publishes a one-page summary of all of this: [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html) (web page) or [PDF](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf). Keep it open while you work on assignments.
:::

## 2. Glimpse the penguins

`glimpse()` is a tidyverse way to inspect a dataset: rows, columns, and column types. Run it on `penguins` from the `palmerpenguins` package so you know which columns to map to axes and colors.

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| setup: true
#| exercise: glimpse_penguins
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| exercise: glimpse_penguins

```

::: {.hint exercise="glimpse_penguins"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?glimpse`: `glimpse(x)` — print a compact summary of a data frame (rows, columns, types).

Example with a built-in dataset:

```r
glimpse(mtcars)
```

Apply the same function to the dataset named in the exercise prompt.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="glimpse_penguins"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
glimpse(penguins)
```

You should see 344 rows and 8 columns. `species` and `island` are `<fct>` (categories); measurements like `body_mass_g` are `<dbl>` (numbers).
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| exercise: glimpse_penguins
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
v <- .last_value
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Is the function spelled `glimpse` and the dataset `penguins`?")
} else if (is.data.frame(v) && nrow(v) == 344) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "344 rows, 8 columns. Now you know which columns can go on an axis or a color.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Run `glimpse()` on the `penguins` table.")
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

From the `glimpse()` output:

1. How many **rows** are there?
2. What **type** is `body_mass_g`?
3. Which column tells you **which island** each penguin was sampled on?

**Answers:** 344 rows; `body_mass_g` is `<dbl>`; `island`.
:::

## 3. Histogram with ggplot2

Start a figure with `ggplot()`, map `body_mass_g` to the x-axis, and add `geom_histogram()`. Use the `penguins` dataset directly — an upgrade from Coding Activity 2's `hist()`. Add a title with `labs(title = "...")`.

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| exercise: ggplot_histogram
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="ggplot_histogram"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?ggplot`: `ggplot(data = NULL, mapping = aes(), ...)` — then add a layer with `+`.

From `?geom_histogram`: bins one continuous variable.

Example:

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Car fuel economy")
```

Map the x-axis to one continuous column from `penguins` and add your own title.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ggplot_histogram"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Penguin body mass")
```

A histogram shows how **one continuous variable** is distributed — how many penguins fall in each weight range. ggplot2 may warn about two rows with missing body mass; that is normal.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| exercise: ggplot_histogram
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
find_plot <- function(v, env) {
  if (inherits(v, "ggplot")) return(v)
  for (nm in rev(ls(env))) {
    o <- get(nm, envir = env)
    if (inherits(o, "ggplot")) return(o)
  }
  NULL
}
layer_class <- function(p, part) vapply(p$layers, function(l) class(l[[part]])[1], character(1))
plot_maps <- function(p) {
  m <- c(as.list(p$mapping), unlist(lapply(p$layers, function(l) as.list(l$mapping)), recursive = FALSE))
  names(m) <- sub(".*\\.", "", names(m))
  m
}
plot_title <- function(p) tryCatch(p$labels$title, error = function(e) NULL)
p <- find_plot(.last_value, .envir_result)
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Layers are joined with `+`, and `aes()` sits inside `ggplot()`.")
} else if (is.null(p)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "No figure yet. Start with `ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g))` and add a geom with `+`.")
} else if (!"StatBin" %in% layer_class(p, "stat")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "A figure, but not a histogram. Add `geom_histogram()` to bin one continuous variable.")
} else if (is.null(plot_title(p))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Histogram drawn. Add a title with `labs(title = \"...\")`.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Histogram with a title: the distribution of one continuous variable.")
}
```

## 4. Scatterplot — two continuous variables

Build a **scatterplot**: flipper length on the x-axis, body mass on the y-axis. Map `species` to **color** so each species gets its own hue. Use `geom_point()`.

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| exercise: ggplot_scatter
ggplot(penguins, aes(
  x = flipper_length_mm,
  y = body_mass_g,
  color = species
)) +
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="ggplot_scatter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?geom_point`: scatterplot of two continuous variables. Map a third variable to `color` inside `aes()`.

Example:

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()
```

Use flipper length and body mass on the axes and map species to color on the penguin data.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ggplot_scatter"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
ggplot(penguins, aes(
  x = flipper_length_mm,
  y = body_mass_g,
  color = species
)) +
  geom_point()
```

Scatterplots relate **two continuous measurements**. Color adds a **third variable** — here, species — so you can see clusters.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| exercise: ggplot_scatter
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
find_plot <- function(v, env) {
  if (inherits(v, "ggplot")) return(v)
  for (nm in rev(ls(env))) {
    o <- get(nm, envir = env)
    if (inherits(o, "ggplot")) return(o)
  }
  NULL
}
layer_class <- function(p, part) vapply(p$layers, function(l) class(l[[part]])[1], character(1))
plot_maps <- function(p) {
  m <- c(as.list(p$mapping), unlist(lapply(p$layers, function(l) as.list(l$mapping)), recursive = FALSE))
  names(m) <- sub(".*\\.", "", names(m))
  m
}
plot_title <- function(p) tryCatch(p$labels$title, error = function(e) NULL)
p <- find_plot(.last_value, .envir_result)
maps <- if (is.null(p)) list() else plot_maps(p)
col_var <- if (!is.null(maps$colour)) rlang::as_label(maps$colour) else NULL
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Check that every `aes()` argument is separated by a comma.")
} else if (is.null(p)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "No figure yet. Keep the `ggplot()` call and add a geom with `+`.")
} else if (!"GeomPoint" %in% layer_class(p, "geom")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "A figure, but no points. Add `geom_point()` for a scatterplot.")
} else if (is.null(col_var)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Points drawn. Map `color = species` inside `aes()` so each species gets its own hue.")
} else if (col_var != "species") {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
       message = paste0("Color is mapped to `", col_var, "`. The prompt asks for `species` so the three clusters stand out."))
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Scatterplot with species as color: two continuous variables plus a grouping.")
}
```

## 5. Boxplot — compare groups

Coding Assignment 2 builds a boxplot **one layer at a time**. Here is the core pattern:

- Put **island** on the x-axis, **body_mass_g** on the y-axis
- Add `geom_boxplot()` with `fill` mapped to island
- Add `theme_minimal()` and readable `labs()`

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| exercise: ggplot_boxplot
ggplot(penguins, aes(
  x = island,
  y = body_mass_g,
  fill = island
)) +
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="ggplot_boxplot"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?geom_boxplot`: compare a numeric variable across groups.

Example pattern:

```r
ggplot(mtcars, aes(
  x = factor(cyl),
  y = mpg,
  fill = factor(cyl)
)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "MPG by cylinder count", x = "Cylinders", y = "MPG")
```

Apply the same layering — boxplot, fill, `theme_minimal()`, `labs()` — to islands and body mass.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ggplot_boxplot"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
ggplot(penguins, aes(
  x = island,
  y = body_mass_g,
  fill = island
)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Body mass by island",
    x = "Island",
    y = "Body mass (g)"
  )
```

Boxplots compare a **continuous variable** across **groups**. On your graded assignment you will add `reorder()` to sort groups by elevation after you join that metadata in Coding Activity 6.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
#| exercise: ggplot_boxplot
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
find_plot <- function(v, env) {
  if (inherits(v, "ggplot")) return(v)
  for (nm in rev(ls(env))) {
    o <- get(nm, envir = env)
    if (inherits(o, "ggplot")) return(o)
  }
  NULL
}
layer_class <- function(p, part) vapply(p$layers, function(l) class(l[[part]])[1], character(1))
plot_maps <- function(p) {
  m <- c(as.list(p$mapping), unlist(lapply(p$layers, function(l) as.list(l$mapping)), recursive = FALSE))
  names(m) <- sub(".*\\.", "", names(m))
  m
}
plot_title <- function(p) tryCatch(p$labels$title, error = function(e) NULL)
p <- find_plot(.last_value, .envir_result)
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Every layer, including `theme_minimal()` and `labs()`, is joined with `+`.")
} else if (is.null(p)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "No figure yet. Keep the `ggplot()` call and add `geom_boxplot()` with `+`.")
} else if (!"GeomBoxplot" %in% layer_class(p, "geom")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "A figure, but no boxes. Add `geom_boxplot()`.")
} else if (length(p$theme) == 0) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Boxplot drawn. Add `theme_minimal()` for a cleaner background.")
} else if (is.null(plot_title(p))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Almost there. Add `labs(title = ..., x = ..., y = ...)` so a reader knows what they are looking at.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Layered boxplot with fill, theme, and labels. Assignment 2 ready.")
}
```

## 6. Recap — ggplot functions you practiced

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What does each function do?

| Function | Role |
|----------|------|
| `library(tidyverse)` | Loads ggplot2 and related packages |
| `glimpse()` | Quick look at rows, columns, and types |
| `ggplot()` + `aes()` | Starts a figure and maps columns to axes, color, or fill |
| `geom_histogram()` | Distribution of one continuous variable |
| `geom_point()` | Relationship between two continuous variables |
| `geom_boxplot()` | Compare a continuous variable across groups |
| `theme_minimal()` + `labs()` | Cleans appearance and adds titles/labels |

If you can explain each row in your own words, you have covered the figure-building core of **Coding Assignment 2**.
:::

## Keep playing

No grading here. Try swapping geoms, mapping a different column to color, or predicting what a plot will look like before you run it.

```{webr}
#| envir: visualize_penguins
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = bill_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Bill length by species", x = NULL, y = "Bill length (mm)")
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Try this with a partner.** One of you predicts the figure; the other runs the code. Swap roles. Saying your prediction out loud first is one of the fastest ways to learn.
:::
